title: The Mind, the Page, and the Falling Tone

lessons.title: ਸੋਚਣਾ (sochṇā) — “to think,” and it once meant “to burn”
lessons.gloss: to think — a verb that started out meaning to burn, and then to grieve

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Āuṇā handed English come outright, and jāṇnā — the one with the doubled n, one letter away from jāṇā “to go” — simply is English know. This verb hands over nothing, and its history is the oddest so far.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਸੋਚਣਾ — sochṇā — to think.

Take off the familiar -ਣਾ and the stem is soch-. That stem stands alone as a noun too: ਸੋਚ soch, “a thought” — and, just as ordinarily, “a worry.” Hold on to that double meaning; the history is about to explain it.
ਸ s, carrying the ੋ sign for o — the horā, a small hook above the letter. Then ਚ ch, a plain ch with no puff of breath. Then the ending ਣਾ. It reads so-ch-ṇā.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — thinking that began as burning

segments.text: sochṇā comes through Prakrit soccaï from Sanskrit śocyate, and behind that stands the root śuc-, whose first meaning is “to burn, to glow.” Its second meaning is “to grieve.”

The sense cooled by stages: burn becomes be eaten up by something becomes brood on it becomes plain think. Punjabi's ordinary word for thinking is an old word for being on fire, which is exactly why soch is a thought and a worry at once.

The same root gives Sanskrit śoka, “sorrow” — and a-śoka, “without sorrow,” which is the name the emperor Aśoka carried. A word for grief sits inside both a Punjabi verb and one of the most famous names in Indian history.
State the limit plainly: śuc- has no secure English cousin. Other verbs gave you one; this one does not, and inventing one would be worse than saying so.

segments.text: What did the root under sochṇā mean first? (To burn, then to grieve.) What famous name is built on it? (Aśoka — “sorrowless.”) Does it have an English cousin? (No.) And which of your earlier verbs is English know? (Jāṇnā, not jāṇā.)

segments.prompt: The Punjabi noun soch means a thought and one other thing. What?

feedback.correct: Right: soch is a thought and a worry, because the root under it meant to burn and then to grieve.
feedback.incorrect: It also means a worry — the root under it, śuc-, meant to burn and then to grieve.

lessons.title: ਸਮਝਣਾ (samajhṇā) — “to understand,” and the tone you can hear in it
lessons.gloss: to understand — from a root meaning “to wake up,” and the word carries a tone

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say sochṇā and name what its root meant first. (To burn, then to grieve.) Now the pair from khāṇā's lesson — kòṛā the horse, koṛā the whip. That dip is about to turn up inside a word.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਸਮਝਣਾ — samajhṇā — to understand.
Strip the -ਣਾ and the stem is samajh-. Like soch, it is also a noun: ਸਮਝ samajh, “understanding, sense.”
ਸ s, ਮ m, then ਝ, then ਣਾ — sa-majh-ṇā. ਝ is new, and it is what this lesson is about.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need — the mirror of the tone rule

segments.text: ਝ is the fourth letter of the ch-row, once jha — a j said with a breathy voice, the kind Punjabi gave up. In ਘੋੜਾ kòṛā it stood first, and the pitch it left was low and rising. Here it sits after the first vowel, and the rule mirrors: the breath goes, and the pitch on the vowel before it goes high and falls.
So ਸਮਝਣਾ (samajhṇā) is written with a jh and said without one. An acute marks that falling pitch, the twin of the grave on kòṛā:

utterances: written: ਸਮਝਣਾ samajhṇā. said: samájṇā, high then dropping.
written: ਖਾਣਾ khāṇā. said: khāṇā, level — ਖ had no voice to lose.

segments.text: Punjabi has been shedding breathy sounds for a long time. Your first verb shows an older round: Sanskrit bhū- had a breathy bh, and ਹੋਣਾ hoṇā comes out with a plain ਹ.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — understanding is waking up

segments.text: samajhṇā continues Sanskrit sambudhyate — sam-, “together,” on budh-, “to wake, to become aware.” To understand is to wake up to something. That root named a person: buddha means “awakened,” the title the Buddha carries.
And budh-'s breathy dh is the very sound that became this word's ਝ: budhyate went to Prakrit bujjhaï and on into samajh-. The falling pitch is the last trace of that root's old breath.
The root is Indo-European, bʰewdʰ-, which English keeps in bode — as in “this bodes well” — and in forebode and forbid.

segments.instruction: the rule — first in the word the pitch rises; later, it falls

segments.text: Where does the pitch fall in samajhṇā, and why? (On the vowel before ਝ, where that letter's old breath went; in kòṛā the letter stood first and the pitch rose instead.) What did budh- mean, and who is named from it? (To wake; the Buddha.)

segments.prompt: In samajhna the jh is not heard as breath. What is heard instead?

feedback.correct: Right: the breath is gone and the vowel before it goes high and falls.
feedback.incorrect: A falling tone. The breath moved onto the vowel before it, which goes high and drops.

lessons.title: ਪੜ੍ਹਨਾ (paṛhnā) — “to read,” which used to mean “to say out loud”
lessons.gloss: to read — and in the language it came from, reading meant saying it out loud

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say samajhṇā as it is actually said, pitch going high and dropping, and name the root behind it. (Budh-, “to wake.”) This verb carries the same fall — and the letter that puts it there sits somewhere new.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਪੜ੍ਹਨਾ — paṛhnā — to read, and also to study.
The stem is paṛh-, and its h is not breath. It is the falling pitch again: páṛnā, high on the vowel and dropping. Punjabi writes this verb both ਪੜ੍ਹਨਾ (paṛhnā) and ਪੜ੍ਹਣਾ; this book uses the first.
ਪ p, then ੜ ṛ — a flapped r made with the tongue tip curled back and struck forward. Then the new thing, then ਨਾ.

Every Gurmukhi letter so far has hung from the top line that runs across a word. ੍ਹ breaks that habit: it is ਹ shrunk and tucked underneath its neighbour, so ੜ plus a subjoined ਹ is written ੜ੍ਹ. Gurmukhi has a small set of these subjoined forms, and this is the commonest.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — reading with the mouth, not the eye

segments.text: paṛhnā comes through Prakrit paḍhaï from Sanskrit paṭhati, and paṭhati has nothing to do with the eye. It means “recites, reads aloud, rehearses, declaims.” Reading was named as something the mouth does.
Set that against your verb for seeing: ਵੇਖਣਾ vekhṇā, whose twin is dekhṇā, is built on the eye itself. Only one of the two is an eye-word, and it is not the reading one.
No dead metaphor: the same root gives ਪਾਠ pāṭh, a recitation of scripture read aloud end to end — and Gurmukhi is the script the Sikh Gurus shaped to carry exactly that.
Where paṭh- itself came from is not settled, so this lesson claims no English cousin for it.

segments.text: What did paṭhati mean? (To recite aloud.) So which organ names Punjabi's reading verb, the eye or the mouth? (The mouth.) And what is unusual about the ਹ in ੜ੍ਹ? (It is subjoined — tucked below, not hung from the top line — and it is heard as a falling pitch, not as breath.)

lessons.title: ਲਿਖਣਾ (likhṇā) — “to write,” which is scratching
lessons.gloss: to write — from a root meaning to scratch, which is how three unrelated languages named it

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say paṛhnā with its falling pitch, and say what paṭhati meant. (To recite aloud.) You can read now. The fourth verb is the other half of that, and then the chapter closes with a sentence you can actually use.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — one word

segments.text: ਲਿਖਣਾ — likhṇā — to write.
The stem is likh-. The ਖ here is a plain aspirated kh, a real puff of breath — no falling pitch anywhere in this word. Two verbs in a row carried a tone; this one does not.

ਲ l, then ਖ kh, then ਣਾ. The short i has a quirk worth knowing: its sign ਿ is written before the letter it is pronounced after, so li comes out as ਲਿ — sign first, consonant second. It still hangs from the same top line as everything else.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — writing is scratching

segments.text: likhṇā is Sanskrit likhati, whose plain meaning is “scratches, scrapes.” Writing was named after what a sharp point does to a surface.

Two other languages reached that picture without help from this one. Latin scrībere also meant “to scratch,” and English borrowed it wholesale as scribe, script, describe, inscription. And English's own write is Old English wrītan, “to scratch, to carve” — what you did to a piece of wood with a knife to make a rune. Three languages, three separate decisions, one idea: writing is cutting a mark into something.
Beyond Indo-Aryan, likh-'s relatives are disputed, so this lesson names none.
Chapter 5 gave you the frame ਮੈਂ … -ਦਾ/-ਦੀ ਹਾਂ. Drop the new stems into it:
[YOU SAY (m.): maiṁ panjābī paṛhdā hāṁ, (f.): maiṁ panjābī paṛhdī hāṁ].
[YOU SAY (m.): maiṁ panjābī likhdā hāṁ, (f.): maiṁ panjābī likhdī hāṁ].

segments.instruction: which verb the ਹਾਂ in those sentences belongs to (hoṇā), and which of its two braided roots that present tense comes from (as-, not bhū-)
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which verb the **ਹਾਂ** in those sentences belongs to (*hoṇā*), and which of its two braided roots that present tense comes from (*as-*, not *bhū-*)]

segments.text: Say “I write Punjabi” in your own gender. Now run the chapter's four verbs back to what their roots meant before they meant anything mental: sochṇā (to burn, then to grieve), samajhṇā (to wake), paṛhnā (to recite aloud), likhṇā (to scratch). Which two of the four are said with a falling pitch? (Samajhṇā and paṛhnā.) And which of them writes its h underneath the letter? (Paṛhnā.)

segments.prompt: What did the Sanskrit root behind likhna mean before it meant to write?

feedback.correct: Right: likhati is to scratch or scrape — and Latin scribere and Old English writan named writing the same way.
feedback.incorrect: To scratch or scrape. Latin scribere and Old English writan named writing the same way.
